### Part B - Subsetting (Accessing) Vectors

<br>

```{r}
grades <- c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84)
names(grades) <- c("Math", "Science", "English", "History", "PE")
```

```{r}
# Access the 3rd element of grades using positional indexing
grades[3]
```
<br>

```{r}
# Access the 1st and 4th element of grades using positional indexing
grades[c(1, 4)]
```

<br>

```{r}
# Access "Science" and "PE" together using their names
grades [c ("Science", "PE")]
```

<br>

```{r}
# Return all elements of grades EXCEPT the 1st and 4th, using
# negative indexing, e.g. grades[-c(...)]
grades[-c(1, 4)]
```

<br>

```{r}
# Use a logical condition to return only the grades that are
# greater than or equal to 85 (hint: grades[grades >= 85])
grades[grades >= 85]
```

<br>

##### Question 5:
##### Negative indexing (grades[-1]) removes an element, while logical indexing (grades[grades >= 85]) filters by a condition.

###### Describe a real situation where you would need negative indexing, and a different situation where logical indexing would be the better tool.
```{r}
# in Negative Indexing, lets say that you have a quiz and your first score was not counted, we can use scores[-1] and then R gives us the score except for the first one. You use it when you know exactly where the thing you want to remove.

# On the other hand, Logical Indexing keeps the only ones that passes the test. You write (grades[grade >= 85]) and then R keeps only the grade that passes.
```

<br>


```{r}
Filter(function(i) { all(i %% c(3,5,7) != 0) }, seq(100))
```

#### Question #8:

##### In the vectors-recycling chunk, z has 6 elements and short has only 2. R still produced an answer instead of an error.

##### Explain, in your own words, what R’s “recycling rule” did to short to make the addition work.

```{r}
# Since z has more numbers than short, you can't add them up, because short runs out of number after the two values, that's where the "recycling rule" happens, where in, it repeats 'short' over and over until it's as the same length as z.
```

<br>

#### Question #9:
##### Now try adding z (length 6) to c(1, 0, 1) (length 3) instead. Does it work cleanly?

```{r}
z + c(1, 0, 1)
```
```{r}
#Yes it works cleanly.
```

<br>

##### Then try adding z to c(1, 0, 1, 1) (length 4). Compare the warning (or lack of one) in each case, and explain what condition determines whether R recycles silently versus with a warning.

```{r}
z + c(1, 0, 1, 1)
```

<br>

```{r}
# the result will still execute but R gives us a warning. It is because R still recycles but silently when the longer vector's length is an exact multiple of the shorter ones.
```

### Part D - Lists: Creating and Subsetting

<br>

##### Create a list called student with these named elements:
##### name = "Maria Santos", age = 20, grades = c(88, 92, 79),
##### is_enrolled = TRUE

```{r}
student <- list(name = "Maria Santos",
age = 20,
grades = c(88, 92, 79), 
is_enrolled = TRUE)
```

<br>

```{r}
student["grades"]
class(student["grades"])
```

<br>


```{r}
# Access the "grades" element of student using double brackets
#  student[["grades"]] -- then check its type with class()
```

<br>

```{r}
student[["grades"]]
class(student[["grades"]])
```

<br>

```{r}
# Access the "name" element of student using the $ operator
```

```{r}
student$name
```

<br>

```{r}
# student, extract just the SECOND grade in the grades vector
```

```{r}
student$grades[2]
```

<br>

##### Question #10:
###### - student["grades"] and student[["grades"]] look similar but return objects of different classes.
###### - Run class() on each and explain the difference in what single-bracket [ ] versus double-bracket [[ ]] return from a list.

<br>

```{r}
class(student["grades"])
class(student[["grades"]])
```

<br>

```{r}
# difference between them is that, Single brackets return  a smaller list. Double brackets reaches inside of the list and returns to the element.
```

<br>

##### Question #11:

###### Why do you think R makes a distinction between [ ] and [[ ]] for lists, but a vector only needs [ ]? Think about what a list can contain that a vector cannot.

```{r}
# Because a vector only holds one kind of simple thing, meaning one bracket is enough. Having a list can hold many things, so R needs [] to get a smaller list and [[]] to get the actual item inside it.
```

### Part E: Critical Thinking Challenge

<br>

```{r}
inventory <- list(
  item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"),
  price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00),
  in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

# Using what you learned in Parts B and D, print only the items (from inventory$item) that are currently in stock (in_stock == TRUE)
```

<br>

```{r}
inventory$item[inventory$in_stock]
```

<br>

```{r}
# A new product "Ruler" priced at 15.00 and in stock (TRUE) need to be added to inventory. Use append() to add "Ruler" to inventory$item, 15.00 to inventory$price, and TRUE to inventory$in_stock. (You will need three separate append() calls, one per vector.)
```

<br>

```{r}
inventory$item <- append(inventory$item, "Ruler") 
inventory$price <- append(inventory$price, 15.00) 
inventory$in_stock <- append(inventory$in_stock, TRUE) 

inventory
```

<br>

##### Question #12:

##### In challenge-1, you combined logical indexing on one vector (in_stock) to filter a different vector (item) inside the same list. Explain, step by step, why inventory$item[inventory$in_stock] works even though item and in_stock are stored as separate elements of the list.

```{r}
# 1. Get the TRUE/FALSE values. inventory$in_stock gives you TRUE, TRUE, FALSE. These tell you which items are available.

# 2. Get the item names. inventory$item gives you "Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"

# 3. Use the TRUE/FALSE values to pick items. R keeps an item when its value is TRUE and skips it when its value is FALSE.

# 4. This works because both lists are the same size and in the same order. The 1st TRUE/FALSE matches the 1st item, the 2nd matches the 2nd, and so on. The filtering works because they match up by position.
```

<br>

#### Conclusion

##### A vector holds only one type of data, like all numbers or all words, while a list can hold different types together. Vectors use [ ] to pick items, but lists use [ ] to get a smaller list and [[ ]] or $ to get the item itself. I would use a vector for a simple set of the same kind of values, like a group of grades. I would use a list when I need to keep different kinds of information together, like a student’s name, age, and grades.
